sections.text: 3 Active Probabilistic Reasoning Task We introduce an active probabilistic reasoning task (Fig . 1 A ) inspired by classical decision-making and K K -armed bandit paradigms ( Lai and Robbins, 1985 ; Daw et al., 2006 ; Najemnik and Geisler, 2005 ; Slivkins, 2019 ; Lattimore and Szepesvári, 2020 ) , but explicitly designed to disentangle sampling from inference . The task is well-suited for modeling at the algorithmic level, and its structure is ”simple” in comparison to many current benchmarks ( Jimenez et al., 2023 ; Sprague et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Mialon et al., 2023 ; Phan et al., 2025 ) . This simplicity, however, is deceiving, as below we find that CoT reasoning is required for LLMs to achieve high performance in this task, and that even leading models still under-perform compared to humans in key aspects of the task. Each trial is an independent game with a variable number of sampling rounds N ∈ { 2 , … , 15 } N\in\{2,\dots,15\} followed by a single inference round in which the agent must commit to a final decision. On each sampling round, the agent selects one of four buttons (A–D) and observes a binary outcome (RED/GREEN); at the start of game g g , exactly one button is biased towards RED, emitting RED with probability α B = 0.9 \alpha_{B}=0.9 , while the remaining buttons are unbiased with α U = 0.5 \alpha_{U}=0.5 . The agent’s objective is to identify the biased button from the sampled evidence and report it in the inference round. Formally, the biased button is a latent variable z g ∈ { 1 , … , 4 } z_{g}\in\{1,\dots,4\} ; at round t t the agent chooses a t ∈ { 1 , … , 4 } a_{t}\in\{1,\dots,4\} and observes x t ∈ { 0 , 1 } x_{t}\in\{0,1\} (with x = 1 x=1 for RED). To promote active information acquisition, between 0 0 and 3 3 buttons are temporarily occluded on each round and thus unavailable. Although this task resembles a K K -armed bandit in its sequential action structure, it differs in computational goal and information structure: unlike standard bandits where choices yield rewards and agents maximize cumulative return via exploration–exploitation, here performance is determined solely by a one-shot final inference choice. Sampling choices carry no reward but only provide evidence about the single latent hypothesis (which button is biased). This separation enables independent assessment of sampling quality and inference quality.

4 Data Collection We collect behavioral data from both human participants and language models. Human participants played an interactive, graphical version of the task 1 1 1 https://ai.trt-bench.org . For language models, we designed an equivalent text-based version of the task, in which LLMs interact via token-defined choices under the same instructions provided to the human players (see Appendix B ). Here we describe in detail the experimental procedures used for humans and language models. Humans. We recruited 50 50 human participants for a 1-hour live in-person competition. All participants provided written informed consent prior to the task and received instructions matching those used to prompt the LLMs (Appendix B ). Participants played multiple independent games with trial lengths sampled uniformly between 2 2 and 15 15 rounds. Of the 50 50 participants, 46 46 completed the full protocol of 100 100 games each, yielding 4,600 4,600 games in total (see Appendix E for individual participant performance profiles). Large language models. We evaluate a broad set of models spanning the current LLM landscape, including both state-of-the-art closed-source systems and competitive open-weight models. The models range from dense to Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures across different sizes and training paradigms: pre-trained, instruction fine-tuned, reasoning, and hybrid-reasoning models ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shoeybi et al., 2019 ; Wei et al., 2021 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2022 ; Shu et al., 2023 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) . Our model selection includes: OpenAI’s gpt 4o mini ( Hurst et al., 2024 ) , gpt 4.1 mini ( OpenAI, 2025a ) , gpt 5 mini ( OpenAI, 2025b ) , and the gpt oss open architectures in both the 20b and 120b parameter variants ( OpenAI, 2025c ) ; several llama models ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Dubey et al., 2024 ) , including variants fine-tuned on human behavioral data ( Binz et al., 2025 ) ; a distilled version of deepseek ( Guo and others, 2025 ) ; Anthropic’s claude sonnet 4 and claude haiku 3.5 ( Anthropic, 2025 ) ; Google’s gemini 2.5 pro/flash and the smaller gemma models ( Comanici and others, 2025 ; Gemma Team, Google DeepMind, 2025 ) ; the qwen family, including the 235B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and earlier dense variants ( Qwen Team, 2025 ; Yang and others, 2025 ) ; and the fully open-source apertus model ( Hernández-Cano and others, 2025 ) , grok 3 mini ( xAI, 2025 ) , and glm 4.5 ( Zeng et al., 2025 ) . Some of the included reasoning models allow for control over reasoning effort (resulting in longer or shorter chain-of-thoughts token sequences); we evaluate their performance for both low - and high-reasoning effort. In all figures, results for the high-reasoning condition are shown with gray bars (see, e.g., Fig. 2 A ) and denoted as Extended Reasoning . For every LLM and reasoning condition, we evaluate a minimum of 1,400 1,400 individual games spanning uniformly the range of 2 2 to 15 15 rounds, amounting to more than 55,000 55,000 games in total. Figure 2: Comparing human and LLM behavior. A: Task performance. Average success rate across trial lengths N ∈ { 2 , … , 15 } N\in\{2,\dots,15\} . We report human performance (green), split into lower 75 % 75\% and top 25 % 25\% of participants and the near-optimal reference agent (PPO sampling + MAP inference) (light blue). For models that support increased reasoning effort, gray overlays indicate the Extended Reasoning condition. Error bars represent standard deviations, computed across trial-cluster means with a uniform distribution over the number of rounds. The vertical line marks chance performance (25%). B: Sampling and inference quality. We quantify sampling quality (left) and inference quality (right) as performance loss with respect to the near-optimal agent (lower is better): inference loss is the gap between the agent and a counterfactual agent that preserves the same sampled evidence but applies MAP at the inference round for the final decision; sampling loss is the gap between this counterfactual MAP agent and the reference agent (PPO + MAP), isolating suboptimal evidence acquisition. Reasoning primarily reduces inference loss, with only modest effects on sampling loss. C: Invalid choices. Fraction of invalid choices during sampling (left) and at the final, inference decision (right). Invalid choices include selecting occluded options, producing tokens outside the valid choice set (A–D), or failing to respond; humans cannot produce invalid choices in the graphical interface. Invalid choices occur more frequently during sampling than at the final decision and are reduced by reasoning.

5 Optimal Agent To evaluate and compare the performance of LLMs and humans, we introduce an optimal agent that provides an upper bound on task performance. In our task, where inference and sampling are explicitly separated, establishing the optimal strategy for inference is straightforward: an agent should select the button with the highest posterior probability of being biased, following a Maximum-A-Posteriori (MAP) decision rule ( Griffiths et al., 2008 ) . This optimal inference strategy is defined as follows; button outcomes are generated by Bernoulli emissions, with the emission probabilities { α B , α U } \{\alpha_{B},\alpha_{U}\} for the biased and unbiased buttons respectively. A single game g g of N N rounds consists of a sequence of choice-evidence pairs ( a 1 : N , x 1 : N ) (a_{1:N},x_{1:N}) together with a latent context variable k ∈ { 1 , … , K } k\in\{1,\dots,K\} . We represent beliefs by the posterior vector ( 𝒑 t ) k ∈ Δ K (\bm{p}_{t})_{k}\in\Delta^{K} . We also define the likelihoods over the latent variable k k and emission rates { α B , α U } \{\alpha_{B},\alpha_{U}\} by ( 𝑳 t ) k ∈ Δ K (\bm{L}_{t})_{k}\in\Delta^{K} . By assuming a uniform prior, we can write down the recursive normative posterior via Bayes’ rule as 2 2 2 See Appendix Section H.2.2 for derivation details. : 𝒑 t = 𝒑 t − 1 ⊙ 𝑳 t 𝟏 ⊤ ​ ( 𝒑 t − 1 ⊙ 𝑳 t ) , ( 𝒑 0 ) k = 1 4 . \bm{p}_{t}=\frac{\bm{p}_{t-1}\odot\bm{L}_{t}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}(\bm{p}_{t-1}\odot\bm{L}_{t})},\hskip 20.00003pt(\bm{p}_{0})_{k}=\tfrac{1}{4}. (1) where ⊙ \odot denotes the Hadamard product. The MAP inference policy at round t t selects the hypothesis with maximum posterior probability: a t MAP := arg ⁡ max k ∈ { 1 , … , 4 } ⁡ ( 𝒑 N ) k . a^{\mathrm{MAP}}_{t}:=\arg\!\max_{k\in\{1,\dots,4\}}(\bm{p}_{N})_{k}. (2) Determining the optimal sampling strategy is substantially more complex. The agent faces two sources of uncertainty: (1) buttons are randomly occluded at each round, restricting the available choice set at time t t , A t ⊆ { 1 , … , 4 } A_{t}\subseteq\{1,\dots,4\} in unpredictable ways, and (2) the total number of sampling rounds N ∈ { 2 , … , 15 } N\in\{2,\dots,15\} is unknown to the agent until the inference round begins. These factors render analytical derivation of the optimal sampling policy non-trivial. Consequently, we employ reinforcement learning to obtain a near-optimal sampling strategy. We train an RL agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) ; see Appendix C for full details. The resulting optimal agent combines the PPO-trained sampling policy with the MAP inference rule at the final decision round. We assume that this agent achieves near-ceiling performance and provides normative benchmarks for both sampling and inference quality .

6 Comparing Human & LLM Behavior To compare human and LLM performance, we employ four complementary metrics that capture distinct aspects of behavior: (1) overall task performance, (2) sampling quality, (3) inference quality, and (4) invalid choice rates. Together, these metrics reveal a broad range of behaviors across LLMs, as well as systematic differences between LLM and human performance. Overall task performance. In Figure 2 A , we quantify overall task performance as the average success rate across all trial lengths ( N ∈ { 2 , … , 15 } N\in\{2,\dots,15\} ), i.e., the fraction of games in which the agent correctly identifies the biased button at the inference round. Despite the task’s simple structure, it induces a broad distribution of performance across both humans and models, and is sensitive to explicit reasoning, with clear gains from extended chain-of-thought (gray vs. colored bars). On average, human participants achieve ≃ 61 % \simeq 61\% success, comparable to the best-performing LLM ( gpt 5 mini ); however, the top quartile of humans exceeds this level by ∼ 7 % \sim 7\% , highlighting wide human variability and a remaining gap between top models and skilled human players. Across models, reasoning LLMs outperform non-reasoning counterparts, attaining higher success rates overall. Success rates increase with game-length only for reasoning models; success rates in low/no-reasoning models remain largely flat, suggesting they largely fail to leverage the additional evidence provided by long games (Appendix D ). Sampling & inference quality. In Figure 2 B , we quantify inference quality by computing the performance gap between each agent and a counterfactual agent that retains the same sampling strategy but applies the MAP inference rule at the final choice. This difference quantifies the performance loss attributable solely to suboptimal inference (right-hand side of Figure 2 B , lower is better). We also evaluate Sampling quality , by comparing this counterfactual agent (which combines the agent’s sampling strategy with MAP inference) against the optimal agent defined above (which combines the RL-trained sampling policy with MAP inference). Since both agents share the optimal MAP inference rule, any remaining performance gap reflects the loss due to suboptimal sampling strategy (left-hand side of Fig. 2 B , lower is better). We find that inference quality varies broadly across LLMs and is strongly correlated (negatively, because the metric is a loss) with overall performance ( r = − 0.99 r=-0.99 ), whereas sampling quality is more homogeneous across LLMs and a weaker predictor of performance ( r = − 0.47 r=-0.47 ; r = − 0.70 r=-0.70 if we include extended reasoning variants). Performance gains from extended reasoning are driven mainly by improved inference: for any given LLM, chain-of-thought reduces inference loss by an amount that largely mirrors the corresponding gain in overall performance. Notably, frontier reasoning models match, and sometimes exceed, humans in inference quality. In comparison, extended reasoning has only modest effects on sampling quality, and while the best reasoning models approach the performance of the lower 75% of human participants, skilled humans (top 25%) still substantially outperform LLMs in their sampling strategies (left-hand side of Fig. 2 B ; skilled humans shown in light green). Invalid choice rates. Finally, in Figure 2 C , we quantify invalid choices as the proportion of choices in which agents produce invalid responses during either sampling or inference. Invalid choices include selecting occluded buttons, generating output tokens outside the valid button vocabulary (A–D), or failing to produce a response altogether. By design, human participants cannot produce invalid choices in the graphical interface, and therefore invalid-choice rates are computed only for LLMs. Overall, we do not observe a statistically significant correlation between invalid choice rates and LLM performance; however, invalid choices are consistently reduced under extended reasoning. Invalid responses tend to occur more often during sampling than during inference, potentially reflecting the changing availability of choices during the sampling rounds.

7 A mechanistic model of latent cognitive variables Figure 3: Model parameters explain human and LLM behavior A : Memory parameter β \beta governs non-optimal evidence-integration, spanning stubborn ( β < 0 \beta<0 ) to forgetful ( β > 0 \beta>0 ) regimes. B : Strategy parameter κ \kappa controls choice stochasticity ( random near κ = 0 \kappa=0 , increasingly rational for large κ \kappa ), fit separately for sampling (left) and inference (right). C : Entropy of Choice-bias vector ω x \omega^{x} captures deviations from internal posterior-driven decisions, fit separately for sampling and inference (more biased for smaller entropy). D : Occlusion Awareness parameter (shown as log ⁡ θ \log\theta ) captures sensitivity to occlusions (invalid choices). E : Model schematic: choices generate evidence that updates a Bayesian posterior p t p_{t} ; memory ( β \beta ) produces a non-optimal information accumulation process h t h_{t} ; strategy ( κ \kappa ) applies an inverse-temperature transformation; bias ( ω \omega ) and awareness ( θ \theta ) modulate the resulting policy π t \pi_{t} . The behavioral metrics above reveal systematic differences across LLMs, but do not identify the processes responsible for them. For instance, reasoning might improve inference by changing a single computation shared across models (e.g., evidence accumulation), by jointly affecting multiple computations within each model (e.g., evidence accumulation and internal biases), or by altering different computations in different models. To resolve these possibilities, we develop and fit a mechanistic model of sampling and inference for both humans and LLMs. The model draws on Bayesian ideal-observer and probabilistic cognition frameworks ( Knill and Pouget, 2004 ; Sanborn et al., 2010 ) and parallels recent views of in-context learning as implicit inference over latent context variables ( Xie et al., 2022 ; Panwar et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , but allows for deviations from an ideal-observer in terms of memory accuracy, choice selection strategy and relative choice bias. The fitted parameters define four interpretable latent cognitive variables: Memory, Strategy, Choice Bias , and Occlusion Awareness placing agents in a cognitive space (Fig. 4 A and schematically in Fig. 1 D ) spanned by the key parameters influencing decision strategy. This approach allows us to interpret key differences across LLMs and humans (Figs. 3 , 4 A ). Memory ( β \beta ). As in traditional accounts of probabilistic inference in neuroscience and sequential sampling models ( Busemeyer and Townsend, 1993 ; Usher and McClelland, 2001 ) , we assume that an agent’s choices are a consequence of a non-optimal memory 𝒉 t ∈ ℝ K \bm{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} ( Gold and Shadlen, 2007 ; Hogarth and Einhorn, 1992 ; Ma et al., 2023 ) and is updated via the mean subtracted likelihood: Δ ​ 𝒉 t := log ⁡ 𝑳 t − ⟨ log ⁡ 𝑳 t ⟩ \Delta\bm{h}_{t}:=\log\bm{L}_{t}-\left\langle\log\bm{L}_{t}\right\rangle (3) (See Appendix H.4.3 for details). After each sampling round, 𝒉 t \bm{h}_{t} is given by 𝒉 t = ( 1 − β ) ​ 𝒉 t − 1 + Δ ​ 𝒉 t . \bm{h}_{t}=(1-\beta)\,\bm{h}_{t-1}+\Delta\bm{h}_{t}. (4) Deviations from optimal recollection of evidence are controlled by the memory parameter β ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] \beta\in[-1,1] . For β = 0 \beta=0 accumulation of evidence is perfect ; for β > 0 \beta>0 the agent is forgetful , leading to late evidence weighing more on choices than early one; and for β < 0 \beta<0 the agent is stubborn , leading to early evidence weighing more on choice than late one. Strategy ( κ \kappa ). After updating its memory state 𝒉 t \bm{h}_{t} based on new evidence, the agent converts 𝒉 t \bm{h}_{t} into an internal posterior 𝒑 ¯ t ∈ Δ K \bar{\bm{p}}_{t}\in\Delta^{K} over which button is biased. We model this memory-to-belief transformation by multiplying 𝒉 t \bm{h}_{t} with a strategy parameter κ x \kappa_{x} and re-normalizing, fit separately for sampling and inference ( x ∈ { s , f } x\in\{s,f\} ). This yields a continuum from near-random behavior ( κ x ≈ 0 \kappa_{x}\approx 0 ) to increasingly MAP-like choices (large κ x \kappa_{x} ) ( Ortega and Braun, 2013 ) : 𝒑 ¯ t x = σ ⁡ ( κ x ​ 𝒉 t ) , \bar{\bm{p}}^{\,x}_{t}=\sigma(\kappa_{x}\bm{h}_{t}), (5) For κ x > 1 \kappa_{x}>1 , differences in accumulated evidence are amplified, producing sharper, more decisive behavior; for κ x < 1 \kappa_{x}<1 they are compressed, yielding a more diffuse posterior. In the limit κ x ≫ 1 \kappa_{x}\gg 1 , the policy becomes effectively MAP-like , whereas κ x ≈ 0 \kappa_{x}\approx 0 yields near-uniform ( random ) choices. The policy for both sampling and inference choices is derived directly from 𝒑 ¯ t x \bar{\bm{p}}^{\,x}_{t} . Choice Bias ( 𝝎 \bm{\omega} ). To dissociate evidence-driven choices from systematic preferences, we include choice biases { 𝝎 s , 𝝎 f } ∈ Δ K \{\bm{\omega}_{s},\bm{\omega}_{f}\}\in\Delta^{K} for the sampling and final choices, respectively ( Gershman, 2020 ; Wei et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ) . These normalized bias vectors act multiplicatively on the internal posterior to rescale the propensity for a choice independently of the sampled evidence. To quantify the strength of the bias in an agent, we compute the entropy of the bias vectors H x ( 𝝎 ) = − ∑ j x ω j x log ( ω j x ) H^{x}(\bm{\omega})=-\sum^{x}_{j}\omega^{x}_{j}\log(\omega^{x}_{j}) . Unbiased agents distribute their choices uniformly in the absence of evidence, corresponding to large bias entropy. While, biased agents systematically favor one or more choices over others, corresponding to small bias entropy. Occlusion Awareness ( θ \theta ). To account for invalid sampling choices, we included the occlusion awareness parameter θ ∈ ℝ > 0 \theta\in\mathbb{R}^{>0} , which like the choice biases acts multiplicatively on the internal posterior (see ‘Policy’ below). We define a multiplicative mask m t , j s m^{s}_{t,j} as: m s t , j = θ − 𝟏 { j ∉ 𝒜 t } , m^{s}_{t,j}=\theta^{-\mathbf{1}\{j\notin\mathcal{A}_{t}\}}, (6) where 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} are the available choices at ( t ) (t) . Large θ \theta values result in an agent that is more occlusion‑aware and avoids choosing occluded buttons while small θ \theta values make the agent more prone to selecting occluded buttons. Policy. Finally, the stochastic policy is obtained by combining the internal posterior , the choices biases , and occlusion awareness . We first define an un-normalized choice preference: 𝒖 t x := 𝒑 ¯ t x ⊙ 𝒘 x ⊙ 𝒎 t x , \bm{u}^{\,x}_{t}:=\bar{\bm{p}}^{\,x}_{t}\odot\;\bm{w}_{x}\;\odot\;\bm{m}^{\,x}_{t}, (7) The preferences are then normalized to obtain the full policy 𝝅 t x = 𝒖 t x 𝟏 ⊤ ​ 𝒖 t x \bm{\pi}^{\,x}_{t}=\frac{\bm{u}^{\,x}_{t}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bm{u}^{\,x}_{t}} from which choices are sampled. The details of the model evaluation are described in Appendix E and full model derivations in Appendix H .

8 Reasoning aligns humans and LLMs The parameters of the mechanistic model provide a compact description of the algorithms implemented by the agents we evaluated on the active probabilistic reasoning task (Fig. 3 ; parameter values are also shown in Appendix J ). Critically, this description is also accurate, as simulations of the mechanistic model based on the fitted parameters reproduce all main features of LLM and human behavior in our task (see Appendix F , Fig. 7 ). We find that two model parameters are strongly related to overall LLM performance. First, the memory parameter β \beta has values close to zero for all the highest performing models, indicating close to perfect accumulation of evidence. Poorly performing models instead tend to have large positive or negative β \beta values, indicating either forgetful or stubborn accumulation of evidence (Fig. 3 A ). Second, the inference strategy parameter, κ f \kappa_{f} , has larger values for better models (Fig. 3 B ). For the best models, we find κ f ≫ 1 \kappa_{f}\gg 1 , implying a strategy that approximates a maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) policy. For models with intermediate performance, κ f \kappa_{f} is closer to 1, meaning that information from the internal posterior is influencing final choices, but less so than expected from an optimal agent. Finally, for models with poor performance, κ f \kappa_{f} progressively approaches zero, implying random choices and an inability to act on the observed evidence. Together, these trends in the memory and strategy parameters contribute to the improvements in inference quality observed in high-performing models (Fig. 2 B ). However, other parameters also show substantial variation across LLMs, but weaker correlations with overall performance. Many poorly performing models, but also some high-performing ones, show substantial choice biases (Fig. 3 C ), which necessarily reduce sampling and/or inference quality. For any given LLM, the strength of sampling and inference biases is typically similar, suggesting a common underlying mechanism. LLMs also vary substantially in their occlusion awareness (Fig. 3 D ), resulting in widely different numbers of invalid choices across LLMs (Fig. 2 C ). Across LLMs, CoT reasoning affects all four model parameters, albeit to different extents (Fig. 3 A-D , gray vs. color bars). In most reasoning LLMs, a higher reasoning effort leads to β \beta values closer to zero, indicating more accurate accumulation of evidence, and larger κ f \kappa_{f} values, indicating a more rational policy on the final choice. Higher reasoning effort also reduces choice biases, during both sampling and inference, and increases occlusion awareness. Nonetheless, none of the tested LLMs can fully reproduce the algorithms employed by the optimal agent (Fig. 3 A-D , blue bars). In particular, the inferred sampling strategy parameters κ s \kappa_{s} are substantially smaller than those for the optimal agent or humans (Fig. 3 B , left). This finding implies that sampling choices in LLMs are consistently less influenced by the observed evidence than the optimal agent, which explains the resulting gap in sampling quality discussed above (Fig. 2 B , left). Overall, CoT reasoning results in an increased alignment between the choice strategies used by LLMs and humans. This increased alignment is best appreciated when mapping each agent onto a location in a Cognitive Space spanned by β \beta and κ f \kappa_{f} (Fig. 4 A , and schematically in Fig. 1 D ). This summary representation shows how CoT pushes LLMs towards strategies that are closer to those used by skilled humans (Fig. 4 A , light green dot) and that result in higher overall performance (Fig. 4 A , background color and contours). Agents embedded by fitted memory β \beta ( stubborn β < 0 \beta<0 to forgetful β > 0 \beta>0 ) and inference strategy κ f \kappa_{f} (more rational for larger κ f \kappa_{f} ). Near-optimal agent not shown ( κ f \kappa_{f} beyond y-axis limits). Shading/contours show predicted success across fitted model ( β , κ f ) (\beta,\kappa_{f}) ; markers show humans (green/light green) and LLMs under low/no reasoning (black border) versus extended reasoning (white border). Reasoning shifts models toward the high-success, human-like regime. B: Latent-variable dynamics. Shows a specific evidence sequence (top row) and resulting round-by-round dynamics of latent variables (lower rows) during a game by gpt oss 20b under high - (left) vs. low -reasoning effort (right). Game-dependent terms (log-likelihood increments Δ ​ h t \Delta h_{t} and the posterior p t p_{t} ) are identical across efforts, while agent-dependent quantities differ: low-reasoning yields a stubborn memory state trajectory h t h_{t} (4th row; β < 0 \beta<0 ) and diffuse policy π t \pi_{t} (5th row; smaller κ f \kappa_{f} ), whereas high-reasoning shows near-optimal memory updates ( β ≈ 0 \beta\!\approx\!0 ) and a sharper, more decisive belief-to-choice mapping (larger κ f \kappa_{f} ).

9 Reasoning shapes latent cognitive variables Beyond summarizing the key features of the algorithms implemented by LLMs and humans, our mechanistic model also reveals latent cognitive variables whose dynamics reflect the operation of the distinct processes driving behavior (Fig. 3 E ). For example, our model implies that the final choice generated by an LLM reflects a policy that is obtained by accumulating all the sampled evidence into the memory , producing a strategy-sensitive internal posterior , and finally combining it with systematic biases. These latent variables provide another view into the effects of CoT reasoning, as exemplified in Fig. 4 B by the round-by-round dynamics of some of the inferred variables for a single game played by gpt oss 20b , under high - (left) versus low -reasoning effort (right). We consider how the latent variables are updated on each round, during a game based on a specific sequence of RED and GREEN outcomes sampled across the four buttons (1st-row from top). Each outcome is transformed into a log-likelihood-ratio increment Δ ​ 𝒉 t \Delta\bm{h}_{t} (2nd-row) that can be accumulated into the optimal Bayesian posterior 𝒑 t \bm{p}_{t} (3rd-row). In our model, the Δ ​ 𝒉 t \Delta\bm{h}_{t} contribute to the memory state 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} (4th-row), which is then transformed into a policy for the final choice 𝝅 t \bm{\pi}_{t} (5th-row). The dynamics of the resulting variables differ prominently across reasoning efforts. First, the memory state ( 𝐡 t \mathbf{h}_{t} ) is much more similar to the Bayesian posterior ( 𝐩 t \mathbf{p}_{t} ) for high- vs. low-reasoning effort. Midway through the example game, the Bayesian posterior switches from favoring button C to favoring button A , a dynamic reproduced by the memory state for high-reasoning (because β ≈ 0 \beta\approx 0 ). For low-reasoning , the memory state is stubborn ( β < 0 \beta<0 ), and continues favoring the initially best option ( button C ) even in light of new evidence towards A . Second, reasoning affects the transformation of the memory into the internal posterior : high-reasoning sharpens this mapping, by favoring the best option on each round and ultimately resulting in a more rational policy ( κ f ≫ 1 \kappa_{f}\gg 1 ). In contrast, low-reasoning weakens the differences between options in the internal posterior , which then results in a more diffuse policy ( κ f \kappa_{f} close to 0 0 ). Such latent variables also amount to concrete, testable hypotheses for mechanistic interpretability, which aims to explain behavior at the implementation level by identifying the circuits and causal pathways that give rise to it ( Wang et al., 2022a ; Hanna et al., 2023 ; Gurnee and Tegmark, 2023 ; Bereska and Gavves, 2024 ; Park et al., 2024b ; Sharkey et al., 2025 ) . Past efforts to understand CoT at the implementation level have yielded limited insights, in part because long reasoning traces expand the space of candidate computations and complicate causal attribution ( Bogdan et al., 2025 ; Macar et al., 2025 ) . Latent variables as in Fig. 4 B (and Appendix Fig. 8 B ), have structure and dynamics that is much richer than the categorical (A–D) outputs required by the task, and as such motivate targeted questions about their representation: whether and where these latent variables are encoded in activations and circuits, which layers instantiate them, and how they evolve over the course of a reasoning chain .

10 Discussion Our goal in this work was to understand whether language models form beliefs and make decisions under uncertainty in a human-like way, and how this alignment is affected by chain-of-thought ( CoT ) reasoning. We argued that answering these questions requires approaches that go beyond evaluating task performance alone, and instead rely on algorithmic descriptions that can isolate similarities and differences in the strategies implemented by different agents. We applied this approach in a novel, active probabilistic reasoning task that disentangles sampling (active evidence acquisition) from inference (evidence integration) and employed a mechanistic model to infer interpretable, latent variables explaining each agent’s behavior. Across LLMs, CoT reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, but its effects are selective: reasoning leads to better performance primarily by improving inference rather than sampling . Mechanistically, improved inference is explained by (i) reduced choice biases ( ω \omega ), (ii) a more MAP-like belief-to-choice mapping (larger inference strategy parameters κ f \kappa_{f} ) and, in strong models (iii) more accurate evidence-integration ( β ≈ 0 \beta\!\approx\!0 ). Together, these effects of reasoning move LLMs toward human-like regimes in cognitive space (Fig. 4 B ); sampling strategies, however, remain sub-optimal, leaving a persistent performance gap relative to skilled human sampling. Surprisingly, CoT reasoning in frontier LLMs leads to better alignment between humans and LLMs on our task than what is achieved by non-reasoning LLMs that were fine-tuned on human behavior from large corpora of cognitive tasks Binz et al. (2025) . Our work suggests a path toward LLM evaluations that measure capability while constraining underlying mechanisms, by asking not only whether models solve a task but how they do so. The resulting compact, algorithmic descriptions of how reasoning changes LLM strategies provides concrete hypotheses for analyses at the implementation-level.
